PASSAGE 1: Read the passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

In many societies, education is spoken of as though it were simply a ladder that individuals climb in order to obtain employment. Students are encouraged to pass examinations, acquire certificates and secure positions that will enable them to earn a living. There is certainly nothing wrong with wanting a useful qualification or seeking a stable career. However, when education is reduced entirely to the pursuit of certificates and employment, an important part of its purpose is lost. Education should not merely prepare people to fit into an existing society; it should also prepare them to understand, question and improve that society.

A person may possess several certificates and still lack the ability to reason carefully. Such a person may remember facts for an examination but struggle to determine whether information encountered outside the classroom is reliable. This distinction has become particularly important in an age in which people are surrounded by enormous quantities of information. A message can be forwarded to thousands of people within minutes, even when its claims have never been verified. Photographs can be altered, statistics can be presented without context, and confident statements can be made to appear authoritative simply because they are repeated frequently. Education that develops judgement therefore has value far beyond the examination hall.

Critical thinking does not mean that a person should reject everything that others say. On the contrary, a critical thinker listens carefully and considers evidence before reaching a conclusion. If a student disagrees with a teacher, for example, the appropriate response is not to dismiss the teacher automatically. The student should ask what evidence supports the teacher's position, examine alternative explanations and determine whether the disagreement is based on facts or assumptions. In this way, education teaches intellectual discipline rather than mere opposition.

The ability to ask good questions is another important part of learning. A student who asks why a particular event occurred may discover relationships that are not immediately obvious. A student who asks how a statistic was obtained may discover that the figure does not mean what it initially appeared to mean. Similarly, asking who produced a piece of information and for what purpose can reveal possible biases. Good questions do not necessarily provide immediate answers, but they prevent people from accepting weak explanations simply because those explanations are convenient.

Unfortunately, examination pressure can sometimes discourage this kind of learning. When students are told that only marks matter, they may concentrate on predicting questions rather than understanding subjects. Some may memorise model answers without knowing why those answers are correct. Others may become afraid of making mistakes and therefore avoid difficult questions altogether. Yet mistakes are often an important part of intellectual development. A student who discovers that an argument is wrong has an opportunity to understand why it failed and to construct a better argument.

This does not mean that examinations are useless. Examinations can provide a practical way of assessing knowledge and skills, especially when they are carefully designed. The problem arises when examination performance becomes the only measure of ability. A student may perform poorly on one particular day because of anxiety, illness or unfamiliarity with the format, even though the student understands the subject well. Conversely, a student who has memorised information effectively may perform impressively without possessing the deeper understanding required to apply that knowledge in a new situation.

Teachers therefore have an important responsibility. They can encourage students to explain their answers rather than merely provide them. They can ask students to compare different viewpoints, identify weaknesses in an argument and apply principles to unfamiliar situations. Such methods may require more time than simple memorisation, but they develop abilities that remain useful after the examination has ended.

Parents and students also have roles to play. Parents naturally want their children to succeed, but constant emphasis on grades can unintentionally communicate that learning itself has little value. Students, for their part, should recognise that genuine knowledge is not always immediately rewarded. A student may spend hours understanding a difficult concept and receive no mark for that effort until much later, when the concept becomes useful in another subject or situation.

Education also has a social purpose. People who understand history, government, science, economics and literature are better equipped to participate thoughtfully in public life. They are more likely to recognise misleading claims, understand competing interests and appreciate the consequences of decisions. A society in which citizens cannot distinguish evidence from propaganda is vulnerable to manipulation, regardless of how many schools or universities it possesses.

The most valuable education, therefore, is not necessarily the education that produces the largest number of certificates. It is education that develops knowledgeable, thoughtful and responsible people. Certificates may open doors, but judgement determines how people behave after they enter those doors. A qualification can show that a person has completed a course of study; it cannot by itself demonstrate wisdom, honesty or the ability to think independently. Those qualities must be developed through continuous learning and reflection.

Ultimately, education should help individuals become capable of asking meaningful questions, evaluating evidence, learning from mistakes and contributing responsibly to their communities. Employment and examinations remain important, but they should be regarded as parts of education rather than its entire purpose. When education succeeds in developing both knowledge and judgement, its benefits extend beyond the individual to the wider society.

PASSAGE 2: Read the passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

A town can change dramatically without its inhabitants immediately recognising the extent of the change. A new road may appear where there was once a narrow path. Shops may replace small family compounds. A school may expand into land that previously contained farms. Gradually, the familiar landscape becomes different, and people begin to describe the transformation as development. Development, however, is not simply a matter of constructing more buildings or increasing the number of vehicles on the road. It is a much broader process involving the quality of people's lives, the opportunities available to them and the ability of a community to meet present needs without destroying its future.

For many communities, development brings undeniable benefits. Better roads can reduce the time required to transport goods and allow people to reach hospitals, schools and markets more easily. Reliable electricity can support businesses and make it possible for students to study after sunset. Improved communication networks can connect small businesses to customers outside their immediate areas. New industries can provide employment and increase government revenue. These changes can transform opportunities for families that previously had very few choices.

Yet development can also create problems when it is poorly planned. A road may make transportation easier while encouraging rapid construction along its edges without adequate drainage. A new market may create employment while producing large amounts of waste that are dumped into nearby waterways. A factory may employ hundreds of people while releasing pollutants that damage the health of residents. A growing population may increase demand for housing while reducing the amount of land available for agriculture. Development therefore involves choices, and those choices have consequences.

One of the most difficult challenges is deciding who benefits from development and who bears its costs. A new commercial centre may create profitable opportunities for landowners, traders and investors. At the same time, tenants may face higher rents and poorer families may be pushed farther away from the centre of economic activity. When a major road is constructed, some property owners may receive compensation for land acquired for the project, while people who depended on informal businesses along the road may lose their sources of income. A project can therefore be economically successful in one sense while producing hardship in another.

This is why planning should involve more than experts working behind closed doors. People who live in an area often possess knowledge that cannot easily be obtained from maps or statistics. They know where flooding occurs after heavy rainfall, which roads become dangerous at night and which community facilities are already overcrowded. Their knowledge does not mean that every local proposal should automatically be accepted, but it does mean that local experience should be considered before major decisions are made.

Public participation also has another advantage: it can increase trust. When people understand why a project is being proposed, how it will be financed and what effects it may have, they are more likely to support it or at least engage with the process constructively. By contrast, decisions made without explanation can produce suspicion. Even a project that has genuine benefits may face resistance if residents believe that information has been hidden from them.

Environmental considerations are equally important. Natural resources are not unlimited, and damage to the environment can be expensive to reverse. A wetland that is filled to create building space may have previously absorbed excess water during heavy rainfall. Removing vegetation from hillsides may increase erosion. Polluting a river may affect fishing, farming and access to clean water. The financial value of a project may therefore look attractive when calculated in isolation, while its long-term environmental cost remains invisible.

Sustainable development seeks to address this problem by considering both present and future needs. It does not mean that communities must reject every new building, factory or road. Rather, it means that development should be planned so that today's improvements do not create unnecessary difficulties for future generations. A factory, for example, can provide employment while also adopting measures that reduce pollution. A city can expand while protecting important drainage channels and green spaces. Economic growth and environmental responsibility do not necessarily have to be enemies.

Education is another important part of development. A community may receive modern infrastructure but still struggle if its people lack the skills needed to use new opportunities. A new industrial park, for instance, may create jobs, but residents may not benefit fully if they lack the technical skills required by the companies operating there. Investment in education and vocational training can therefore help communities participate more effectively in economic change rather than simply observe it.

Health should also be considered. Economic activity that increases income but creates unsafe living conditions cannot be regarded as successful development in the fullest sense. Clean water, sanitation, waste management and access to healthcare are essential components of a healthy community. When these services are ignored, economic gains may be accompanied by diseases and other social costs that eventually reduce productivity.

Technology has introduced another dimension to development. Digital services can make banking, education, commerce and communication more accessible. A small business can advertise products to customers in distant locations without maintaining a physical shop in every town. Students can access educational materials that were previously unavailable to them. However, technology can also deepen inequality if some people have reliable internet access while others cannot afford suitable devices or data. Development that depends heavily on technology must therefore consider digital access as well.

The success of development should consequently be measured by more than the number of projects completed. A government may proudly announce that hundreds of buildings have been constructed, but the more important questions are whether those buildings serve genuine needs, whether they are maintained and whether ordinary citizens experience improvements in their lives. A road that is completed quickly but deteriorates after a short period may be less valuable than a carefully constructed road that remains useful for decades.

There is also a moral dimension to development. Decisions about land, resources and public money affect real people. Officials who approve projects should therefore consider not only what is profitable or politically attractive but also what is fair. Investors have legitimate interests, but so do residents. Governments need revenue, but citizens also need clean environments and reliable public services. Development becomes meaningful when economic progress is accompanied by fairness, accountability and concern for human welfare.

Ultimately, a developed community is not simply one with tall buildings, busy roads and modern technology. It is a community in which people have meaningful opportunities, essential services are accessible, resources are managed responsibly and citizens have some voice in decisions that affect their lives. Physical infrastructure is important, but infrastructure should serve human beings rather than become an end in itself. The true measure of development is therefore not how dramatically a place changes, but whether the changes produce a healthier, fairer and more sustainable society.
